In a developed country most of the work of the farm is done by machines, so a few workers can cultivate a large area. At the same time industry and services offer better paid work, and these draw people away from farming. Hence the share of population engaged in agriculture is low.

In a village the chief occupation is farming, so most of the land is under crops, and the rest is taken up by things farming needs - pasture for cattle, threshing floors, farm ponds, wells, cattle sheds and field paths. Houses cover only a small part. So rural land use is related to agriculture.

Extensive agriculture is carried on over very large holdings with machinery and a small labour force, and a single crop is grown. The family cannot consume such a large output, so the whole produce is sold in the market for profit. That is why it is a commercial type of agriculture.

An industry needs raw material, power, water, capital, skilled labour, transport and a market together. Very few parts of the world have all of these, and they are found together mainly in Western Europe, eastern North America, Japan and parts of Asia. Hence industries are concentrated in a few regions and the distribution is uneven.

The Panama Canal cuts through the narrow isthmus of Central America and joins the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean. A ship sailing from the east coast of America to the Pacific no longer has to go round Cape Horn, and is saved thousands of kilometres. As the canal is the doorway through which ships enter the Pacific, it is called the gateway to the Pacific.

Relief, climate, soil, water and minerals decide which activities are possible in a region at all. Level land, adequate water, fertile soil and minerals allow farming, industry and transport to develop, while rugged, dry or barren land does not. Since the physical setting sets the limit within which every other factor works, it is the most important for regional development.

Donor region: the region people move OUT of. Its population falls, it loses people of the working age group and often the men, its sex ratio and age structure become unbalanced and labour grows short.
Recipient region: the region people move IN to. Its population rises and it gains workers, but housing, water, transport and other services come under pressure and slums may grow.

Rural settlement: small in size and population; the chief occupation is farming or another primary activity; houses are few and simple; land use is mostly agricultural; services are few; life is closely knit.
Urban settlement: large in size and population; occupations are secondary, tertiary and quaternary; buildings are many, tall and closely packed; land use is mixed and specialised; services are many; life is impersonal.

Horticulture: the growing of fruits, flowers, vegetables, spices and ornamental plants; the holding may be fairly large; the produce may be sent to distant markets and some of it is processed.
Market gardening: the intensive growing of perishable vegetables, fruit and flowers on very small plots near a city; heavy use of manure, irrigation and labour; the produce is taken to the city market fresh every day.

Heavy industries: use bulky, heavy raw material and produce bulky goods, as in iron and steel, shipbuilding and cement; need very large capital, much power and water, and are located near raw material.
Light industries: use small quantities of light raw material and produce light goods, as in electronics, watches and cosmetics; need less capital and power, and are usually located near the market or a skilled workforce.

Physical geography: studies the natural environment - relief, climate, soil, water, plants and animals; its branches are geomorphology, climatology, hydrology, soil geography and biogeography.
Human geography: studies people and their activities - population, settlements, economic activities, society and politics; its branches are population, settlement, economic, social, political and historical geography.

Climate is the strongest physical control on where people live.
Areas of moderate temperature and reliable rainfall, such as monsoon Asia and Western Europe, support farming and carry dense populations.
Very cold areas such as the polar lands and Siberia, and very dry areas such as the Sahara and Central Australia, cannot support crops and are almost empty.
The hot, wet equatorial belt has dense forest, leached soil and disease, so it too is thinly peopled.
So the belts of moderate climate hold most of mankind, and the extremes of cold, drought and equatorial heat hold very few.

By ownership, industries are of four kinds.
Private sector: owned and run by an individual or a company for profit, as in Reliance or Tata industries.
Public sector: owned and run by the government, as in Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited or Hindustan Aeronautics Limited; the aim is service as much as profit.
Joint sector: owned partly by the government and partly by private owners, as in Maruti Udyog in its early years.
Co-operative sector: owned by the producers themselves, who supply the raw material and share the profit, as in the sugar and dairy co-operatives of Maharashtra and Gujarat.

Water transport carries goods over seas, rivers, lakes and canals.
It is the cheapest means for heavy and bulky goods such as coal, ore, grain and oil, because the water itself bears the weight and no track has to be built.
It is the slowest means, it cannot reach inland places, it depends on ports and on the depth of the channel, and it can be stopped by storms or by ice.
Inland waterways use rivers and canals; ocean routes such as the North Atlantic route carry the greatest share of world trade. Canals such as the Suez and the Panama have shortened these routes greatly.

Regional imbalance is reduced by deliberately developing the backward region.
Strategies used: providing infrastructure - roads, railways, power and water; providing public goods and services - schools, colleges, hospitals and drinking water; giving a stimulus to private investment through tax concessions, cheap land in industrial estates and subsidies; developing agriculture through irrigation, seed and credit; creating employment through schemes such as MGNREGA; and setting up growth centres so that development spreads outward from them.
The purpose of all of these is to raise the quality of population and the capacity of the region, so that it can grow on its own afterwards.

Geography studies the earth as the home of people, and explains why one place differs from another.
Its nature is dualistic, because it studies the physical environment and human activity together and is both a natural and a social science.
It is spatial, since it always asks where a thing is and why it is there. It is integrating, since it draws on geology, economics, sociology and other subjects. It is dynamic, since the earth and human activity both keep changing. And it works at every scale, from a village to the whole world.

Agriculture is of several types, and they differ in the size of the holding, the purpose of the crop and the amount of labour and machinery used.
The main types are subsistence agriculture, which is of two kinds - primitive or shifting agriculture and intensive subsistence agriculture; commercial agriculture, which includes extensive commercial grain farming, plantation agriculture, mixed farming, dairy farming, market gardening and truck farming; and specialised types such as horticulture, floriculture and viticulture.
Shifting agriculture is practised in the tropical forests of Africa, South America and North-East India. A patch of forest is cleared and burnt, mixed crops are grown on the ash for two or three years with a hoe or a digging stick, and when the soil is exhausted the plot is abandoned and a new one cleared. Holdings are tiny, no manure or machinery is used, yields are low, and the whole crop is eaten by the family. It is known by local names such as jhum in India and milpa in Central America.
Plantation agriculture is the opposite. It is practised on very large estates in the tropics, mainly in Malaysia, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Brazil and Assam. A single cash crop such as tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane or oil palm is grown with heavy capital, hired labour, scientific methods and a processing factory on the estate itself. The entire produce is meant for export, so the estate depends completely on the world market.

The Demographic Transition Theory explains how the birth rate and the death rate of a country change as it develops, and how its population grows through the stages of that change.
First stage, high stationary: both the birth rate and the death rate are high, because of poverty, illiteracy, disease, famine and the absence of medical care. The two cancel each other, so the population is nearly stationary. No country is fully in this stage today; some tribal societies are close to it.
Second stage, early expanding: the death rate falls sharply as food supply, water, sanitation and medical care improve, but the birth rate stays high because habits, beliefs and the value placed on a large family do not change as quickly. The gap between the two widens and the population grows very fast. This is the stage of population explosion, seen in parts of Africa and earlier in India.
Third stage, late expanding: the birth rate now begins to fall too, as literacy and urbanisation spread, women work outside the home, children become costly to raise and family planning is accepted. The death rate is already low, so the gap narrows and growth slows although it continues. India and China are in this stage.
Fourth stage, low stationary: both rates are low and nearly equal, so growth is very slow and the population becomes stable. Western Europe and Japan are here.
A fifth stage, declining, is now recognised, in which the birth rate falls below the death rate because of very small families and a large elderly population, so the total population begins to decline, as in Germany, Japan and Russia.
The theory is useful because it links population growth to the level of development, but it is based on the experience of Western countries and does not fit every country exactly.
